title: The Inverse of a Square Matrix Flashcards

cards.front: What is the definition of the inverse of a square matrix $A$?
cards.back: A matrix $A^{-1}$ such that $AA^{-1} = I$ and $A^{-1}A = I$, where $I$ is the identity matrix.

cards.front: When does a square matrix have an inverse?
cards.back: When its determinant is not zero (or equivalently, when it is row-equivalent to the identity matrix). Such a matrix is called invertible or nonsingular.

cards.front: How do you find the inverse of a matrix using Gauss‑Jordan elimination?
cards.back: Form the augmented matrix $[A \mid I]$, then row reduce until the left side is $I$. The right side becomes $A^{-1}$.

cards.front: What does it mean if the left side of $[A \mid I]$ cannot be reduced to $I$?
cards.back: The matrix $A$ is singular, meaning it does not have an inverse.

cards.front: State the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}$.
If the determinant of a $2 \times 2$ matrix is zero, what can you conclude?
cards.back: The matrix is singular; it has no inverse.

cards.front: How can you verify that matrix $B$ is the inverse of matrix $A$?
cards.back: Check that $AB = I$ and $BA = I$. Both products must equal the identity matrix.

cards.front: What is the product of a matrix and its inverse?
Is the inverse of a nonsquare matrix defined?
cards.back: No. Only square matrices can have inverses.

cards.front: How do you use an inverse matrix to solve a system $AX = B$?
cards.back: If $A$ is invertible, multiply both sides on the left by $A^{-1}$: $X = A^{-1}B$.

cards.front: Why must you multiply $A^{-1}$ on the left of $B$ when solving $AX = B$?
cards.back: Matrix multiplication is not commutative; $A^{-1}(AX) = (A^{-1}A)X = IX = X$, so $X = A^{-1}B$. Multiplying on the right would give $AXA^{-1}$, which is not $X$.

cards.front: If a square matrix $A$ is singular, how many solutions can the system $AX = B$ have?
cards.back: Either no solution or infinitely many solutions, but not a unique solution.

cards.front: In the Gauss‑Jordan inverse method, what is the first step?
cards.back: Adjoin the identity matrix to the right of $A$ to form $[A \mid I]$.
